summary: Describes an architectural framework for controlling media servers. It defines the logical entities involved, their naming conventions, and how they interact. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Media servers play and mix sounds and videos for calls, and other machines tell them what to do. This note names the parts and how they cooperate.

subtitle: The blueprint for application servers to command media servers

tldr.problem: Application servers need to control media servers that process audio and video, but there was no standard architectural framework for how they should interact.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines logical entities, naming conventions, and interactions between application servers and media servers, using SIP for both session establishment and control channels with TCP or SCTP for reliable message delivery.
tldr.outcome: A standardized architecture that enables applications like IVR and conferencing to control media processing on network servers.

facts.label: Security for control
facts.value: TLS (required to implement, optional in deployment)

today: RFC 5567 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a normative reference for media server control architecture and has influenced the design of media control protocols like RTSP and H.248.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Applications sometimes need to process media streams—playing announcements, mixing multiple callers, or detecting button presses on a phone. Rather than doing this work on the application server itself, a separate Media Server handles the actual media processing. The application server sends high-level commands to the media server and receives status updates back.

This document provides a reference architecture describing how application servers and media servers talk to each other. It defines what functional entities exist, what they are called, and how they interact using SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) for both establishing media sessions and creating control channels for commands.
sections.plainLanguage: When a program needs to play a message or record a call, it talks to a specialized machine. This describes what that conversation looks like.

sections.title: The Three Entities
sections.content:
The architecture centers on three main roles: the Application Server runs the business logic and hosts communication applications; the Media Server performs media processing functions such as mixing, transcoding, DTMF detection, and recording; and User Agents (like SIP phones) send media directly to the media server but send signaling to the application server.

The application server uses two types of SIP dialogs to interact with the media server. An MS Control Dialog establishes a reliable control channel (using TCP or SCTP) over which the application server sends commands and the media server sends responses and notifications. An MS Media Dialog is used to set up the actual media sessions between user agents and the media server, such as when a call needs to connect to an IVR system or a conference.
sections.plainLanguage: Three participants are in the conversation: the boss computer (application server) that makes decisions, the media worker (media server) that does the actual work, and the person on the phone.

sections.title: Commands, Responses, and Notifications
sections.content:
Interaction between application and media servers is based on three message types. Commands are requests from the application server asking the media server to perform or configure a function—for example, 'play this announcement' or 'mix these two callers'. Responses come from the media server reporting on command status, indicating whether the operation succeeded or failed. Notifications are asynchronous messages from the media server reporting results or status changes—for example, 'the user pressed 5' or 'the announcement finished playing'.

The RFC specifies that implementations must support TCP for the control channel and may support SCTP. UDP is not suitable because the media server control protocol requires reliable, sequenced message delivery. The RFC also requires support for TLS as a transport-level security mechanism, though its use in deployments is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss gives orders, the worker reports back on success or failure, and the worker shouts out updates when interesting things happen. They use a guaranteed delivery method so nothing gets lost.

sections.title: Two Major Use Cases
sections.content:
Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems use media servers to play announcements, detect DTMF (phone button) input, record messages, and perform transcoding. Simple IVR services that require no mid-call control can be invoked with just a SIP request. More complex services—such as 'play-and-collect' where a user hears an announcement and must enter digits, or speech recognition scenarios—require the application server to interact with the media server over the control channel throughout the call.

Conferencing systems use the media server as a mixer: it receives media streams from multiple participants and combines them into a conference mix, sending each participant an appropriate mix of the other participants' audio and video. The application server acts as a conference 'focus', directing media into the mixer and controlling which streams are mixed together, their layout, levels, and whether participants can send (using SIP Third-Party Call Control). The architecture also supports floor control, allowing the application server to enforce rules about who can speak at any given moment.
sections.plainLanguage: Two common jobs: IVR asks 'Press 1 for English' and listens for button presses, while conferencing lets many people talk at once by carefully mixing their voices so everyone hears everyone else.

sections.title: Security and Resource Protection
sections.content:
Media servers are valuable network resources that must be protected against unauthorized access. The architecture leverages SIP's built-in security mechanisms for authentication and identity: only authorized application servers can establish control channels to a media server or initiate media sessions. TLS protects the control channel to ensure the integrity of control messages, preventing tampering with commands that affect service and resource consumption.

Because media servers may be shared by multiple application servers, the architecture requires that media servers prevent one application server from accessing resources allocated by another. This is typically achieved by associating resource ownership with the application server that originally allocated it and verifying that subsequent requests for that resource come from the same application server.
sections.plainLanguage: The media server needs a lock on the door so only authorized bosses can give orders, and a log to make sure each boss only manages their own calls.
